newsitem.title: CANADA: Clock winds down in Canadian Air rescue talks.
newsitem.headline: Clock winds down in Canadian Air rescue talks.

text.p: Last-ditch talks aimed at keeping Canadian Airlines Corp. aloft intensified on Tuesday as the clock wound down to a Wednesday deadline for all parties to agree to the ailing carrier's survival plan.
A deal appeared to be taking shape that would include tax breaks for the airline from the governments of Canada, Alberta and British Columbia.
There was also speculation that Calgary-based Canadian, Canada's second biggest airline, might scale back its proposed employee wage cut to five percent from 10 percent.

Four of the company's unions have agreed to most of Canadian's three-pronged life-support strategy on the condition that requests for government involvement -- which management rejected at the outset of its public financial crisis -- be explored.

The plan includes the controversial 10 percent wage cut for Canadian's 16,400 employees, major route restructurings and a C$48 million ($36 million) reduction in computer and management fees paid to 33 percent-owner AMR Corp., the parent of American Airlines.
It is aimed at improving cash-poor Canadian's bottom line by C$180 million ($135 million) a year over the next four years.
Two of Canadian's biggest unions, the Canadian Auto Workers and Canadian Union of Public Employees, have refused to accept the proposed wage cuts despite the looming deadline.
Canadian Chief Executive Kevin Benson has said the carrier faced financial failure early next year unless it implemented its plan.

CAW negotiator Peggy Nash said in Vancouver that no more meetings were scheduled between the two unions opposed to the restructuring plan and the government or the company. But she agreed that time was running out.
The deadline and Canadian's financial woes "are certainly real," she said.

Benson, who has been in round-the-clock negotiations in Vancouver for the past week, told employees that Canadian's self-imposed November 27 deadline to approve the restructuring package remained firm.

"We have to make some decisions about payments due to creditors at the end of the month. Those decisions cannot be made in five minutes and therefore we believe by November 27 we need a clear indication of where we're going," he said.
He also said Fort Worth, Tex.-based AMR would not agree to reduced fees until Canadian's employees signed on to the plan.
"We will be very focused on getting American's participation," Benson said. "But they are disinclined to consider our plan until we have employees on side."

Bob Rae, adviser to the International Association of Machinists and a former premier of Ontario, said the final push for a deal was on. "We basically have 48 hours to make some decisions...and those are the 48 hours that are going to tell the story."
